My car is chevy cobalt and the manual says the car will tell me when to change the oil based on revolutions and temperature not based on mileage. My question is how accurate is it? I don't want to burn my engine up, but at the 3,000 mile mark the car claims it has another 5,000 miles before it needs an oil change. Am I just a really good driver and not being hard on the engine or is the car underestimating how much it needs oil?

In Canada the old rule of thumb was every 5,000 Km. Nowadays though, I'm seeing 10,000 Km a lot. I have a diesel pickup (2001 sierra) and it says every 10,000 Km. I change it every 5,000 Km anyways.

More frequently is only going to cost your more money and if anything, it's better for you motor.

Had a 2005 cobalt. Changed mine every 5k or 6 months, whichever came up first. Cobalts should be using full synthetic oil so this isn't a bad interval. Newer vehicles (2010ish onward) are mostly designed to go 10k or 1 year but most people I know still aren't comfortable with service intervals this long. 5k/6 months if you want to drive that thing till the wheels fall off.
Source: Service Adviser at a Volkswagen dealership.
I have it done once a year, which is about every 20K kms. (~12K miles)
You should definitely do it about twice as often.

If you use quality synthetic oil and a quality oil filter you can go 15,000 miles on a change. 8,000 miles is about right for budget synthetic oil and a budget oil filter. My cars service light, which indicates to change the oil, blinks at 8,000 miles as a warning, and comes on permanently at 10,000 miles.

My trusty mechanic explained to me that it's the filters that break down before the oil. So at the very least switch the filter every 5k miles. He recommends 3,500 mile oil changes, especially on cars not using synthetic.

For older cars using conventional oils, the general rule was every 3,000 miles for most drivers depending on how the vehicle is used. If you look in the back of your owner's manual there is a maintenance section which details what basic services are needed and when to do them. you will see there is a "normal use" schedule, and a more stringent "severe use" one. If you read the definitions of them, most people will find they fall under the "severe use" definition, since such things as making short frequent trips that do not allow the engine to become fully hot qualify as severe use (because moisture contamination of the oil never fully boils away, for one thing).

Newer vehicles generally require less frequent oil changes for several reasons. First, engines are built to much tighter internal tolerances and engine sealing technology has improved; this reduces combustion blowby past the piston rings and contamination from internal coolant weepage from head gaskets for one thing. Second, modern engine oils, particularly synthetics, are highly engineered and much better at what they are designed to do than they were years ago. Synthetic oils disperse and hold contaminants in suspension much better, reducing engine sludging. They maintain viscosity much better over a high range of temperatures. Other additives such as anti foaming agents and detergents in the oil are much more effective than they were in past years.

The oil life systems used in many newer cars monitor your driving habits, and adjust the recommended oil change interval based on how rapidly the engineers calculate the oil will become contaminated and lose it's effectiveness under the conditions it is being used. As long as you change it at least within that window, you will not void your warranty and in theory your engine will be fine. Note: This also assumes that whoever performs your maintenance service remembers to reset it when they change the oil.

Also, the maintenance reminders assume that the oil being used meets factory specifications. Every manufacturer has their own set of oil specifications, and not all oils meet every spec. All new GM vehicles require oil meeting Dexos specification, and all are synthetics. Ford recommends a specific synthetic blend for most of their vehicles, and many require oils that meet other specs which are full synthetics. All Chrysler vehicles manufactured within the last 10 years or so require oils meeting Chrsler spec MS6395, which are all synthetics (and not all synthetics meet this spec). WV has several oil standards, the most common in the US is VW spec 502.00 and there are very few oils in the US that meet this standard (Mobil-1 for example, does not, but some Castrol and Havoline synthetics do).

If you want your engine to live it's fully designed livfe without major issues or premature wear, you may want to make sure the place changing your oil is using oil that meets your vehicle's specifications. You may be amazed to learn that many oil change places and many mechanics don't even bother to check; they just use whatever brand they have in stock that they buy at a good price. If you go to the manufacturer's sites for the different oil brands, you will find technical specifications and lists of what vehicle manufacturer standards they are certified to meet.

I have kept giant centipedes, snakes, scorpions, and lizards for almost ten years. AMA
Why did you start keeping them? and why those animals?

The whole thing started with snakes. Snakes have always been my favorite animals; their variety is staggering, they're beautiful, and their physiology is incredibly interesting to me -- heat sensitive pits on some species, ectothermic, keeled scales to make sandpaper-like sounds (Echis), and all of the other interesting adaptations. After acquiring three snakes, I ended up becoming interested in Scolopendra due to their appearance, as something about their large size and variety drew me in. I quickly discovered that their behavior, especially their hunting, is incredibly interesting, which led me to acquire more centipedes. I have to also admit, as stupid as it makes me sound, their poor temper and venom makes them even more interesting.

Luckily, no. It was always a huge fear though, especially with the centipedes because they are venomous and very quick to use said venom. While usually not deadly, with smaller animals like cats, it could easily cause a fatal complication. Worst I've had is a single king snake escape, but he didn't go far so I caught him within the hour.
Whats the most dangerous kind of creature you own?

I no longer have her, as she passed away after about four years in my care and who knows how many years in the wild before the person I took her from purchased her. She was a Scolopendra subspinipes and was unusually active for the species, and would often attack anything that moved. S. Subspinipes is also the most venomous animal that I have ever owned, so that crazy attitude mixed with the venom definitely made her the most dangerous. My first thought was that the cost and time associated with keeping these animals would be prohibitive. Have you found any problems with this? If it does not require too much of list, how many of each do you have?

My collection was never huge or anything - some people have hundreds, and mine isn't impressive compared to others. But because it might be interesting (or depressing) I'll do a cost breakdown of what my collection costs in terms of upkeep. So the snakes are the largest money sink, and at this moment I have three of them. One eats once a week and the others eat once every two weeks. So it actually only costs (this is very rough) about 8 dollars a month to feed the three snakes. The crested gecko food only costs about 9 dollars every couple of months for food. I currently don't have any centipedes, but at one point I had five. Feeder insects are very cheap, and once I had a colony going the cost was almost negligible. That isn't to say that these animals are cheap though. I have had vet visits that costed hundreds, and suitable enclosures have been the largest money drain - definitely more than 1,500 has been spent setting up enclosures, but I don't know the exact figure. Maybe time would be an issue for huge collections, but for mine I have not had a problem. I'll use common names for the list of things I have/had: One desert hairy scorpion, two giant Vietnamese centipedes, two Haitian centipedes, one tiger centipede, one Colombian boa, one brazilian rainbow boa, one California kingsnake, one crayfish (I don't know why), four mantises of varying species, and I have a colony of millipedes right now.
That's not too bad at all! Thanks for taking the time to share with us...its truly fascinating :)

Are any of them venomous? Is there a quick way to identify those that are? It's not like I'm scared or anything...

All of the centipedes I have kept are venomous (well, all centipedes are venomous). The best way to identify whether or not a centipede is dangerous is to look up the species native to your area. As far as I know, every Scolopendra species is venomous but the potency varies; I had a polymorpha (tiger centipede) which would not be problematic at all, but the subspinipes would probably send you to the hospital. Luckily, these more nasty tropical varieties aren't very common at all outside of the (duh) tropics. It's also very rare to see centipedes out and about, they're reclusive and nocturnal -- so don't worry. :)

Because they're fascinating, that's pretty much it.

Centipede hunting behavior is the most interesting to me. I've found that after the first few nights in a new enclosure, they'll do their roving in more of a pattern rather than randomly. It's also interesting that if something slightly touches their rear end, they'll flip that end independent of the front and grasp whatever touched them with their legs before curling back around and injecting venom. The hunting dance is my favorite though, when they bob their front end up and down with antennae flicking all over - it's beautiful.

And the lizards are crested geckos, which are very docile and friendly. Only when they're frightened will they make sounds or run away.
